title: Hexagrammum Mysticum: The 60-Pascal-Line Configuration

problemStatement.formal: \text{Given six points on a non-degenerate conic, define } \mathrm{HexagonLabeling} := \mathrm{Sym}(6) / D_6 \text{ (with } D_6 \text{ acting by cyclic rotation and reversal). Then } |\mathrm{HexagonLabeling}| = 60, \text{ and each labeling determines a Pascal line. The 60 Pascal lines pass through 20 Steiner points (3 lines each) and 60 Kirkman points (3 lines each).}
problemStatement.plain: Can the 60-Pascal-line configuration (Hexagrammum Mysticum) be formalized in Lean 4, including the Steiner point count (20) and Kirkman point count (60)?
whyMatters: The Hexagrammum Mysticum is one of the most intricate classical configurations in projective geometry (Steiner 1827, Kirkman 1849, Cayley 1849, Salmon 1879). Six points on a conic produce 60+20+60+15+15 distinct geometric objects with a rich incidence structure.

The parent gallery entry `pascals-hexagon` (Wiedijk #28) already proves Pascal's theorem itself (modulo the Cayley-Bacharach axiom for general conics). This OQ extends the formalization to the full 60-line configuration.

Modern treatment by Conway and Ryba (2012) exposes the configuration via the outer automorphism of S_6 — the only finite simple group of order > 60 with a non-trivial outer automorphism. This gives a beautiful combinatorial framework for the 20 Steiner and 60 Kirkman triples.

proven: Pascal (1639): the basic Pascal's theorem — six points on a conic produce a single Pascal line per cyclic ordering.
Steiner (1827): there are exactly 60 distinct Pascal lines.
Steiner (1827): there are 20 Steiner points (3 Pascal lines through each).
Kirkman (1849): there are 60 Kirkman points (3 Pascal lines through each).
Cayley (1849): the 20 Steiner points lie on 4 'Cayley lines' (5 Steiner points each).
Salmon (1879): the 15 Plücker lines pass through 4 Kirkman points each, and the 15 Salmon points are concurrences of Plücker lines.
Conway-Ryba (2012): combinatorial reformulation via the S_6 outer automorphism, yielding the 20 Steiner triples as 'syntheme totals'.
In-tree: `pascal_hexagon_theorem` (parent gallery entry) — the basic Pascal collinearity (modulo `conic_implies_pascal_constraint` axiom).
open: OQ-03-OQ-01: `card_hexagonalGroup = 12` — establish the dihedral subgroup `⟨hexRot, hexRev⟩` of `Sym(6)` has order 12.
OQ-03-OQ-02: `pascalLine` map well-defined on `Sym(6) ⧸ D_6` (cyclic rotation cycles `(P, Q, R)`; reversal swaps two of them; both preserve collinearity hence the Pascal line).
OQ-03-OQ-03: `steiner_count_eq_20` — enumerate the 20 Steiner triples + prove concurrence for one representative (rest follow by `S_6`-symmetry).
OQ-03-OQ-04: `kirkman_count_eq_60` — enumerate the 60 Kirkman triples + prove concurrence for one representative.
OQ-03-OQ-05 (optional): Cayley lines (20-point on 4 lines), Plücker lines (60-point on 15 lines), Salmon points (15).
knownResults.goal: Statement and proof of the four sub-OQ count theorems: `card_hexagon_labelings = 60`, `steiner_count_eq_20`, `kirkman_count_eq_60`, plus a well-defined `pascalLine : HexagonLabeling → ProjLine` map.

insights: S3c-prep-2 (researcher-3, 2026-05-12): The ZMod 6 wraparound in (i + j).val ≡ i.val + j.val [MOD 6] and the orderOf_hexRot = 6 fact compose cleanly: ZMod.val_add gives the % 6, pow_mod_orderOf collapses it. This is the same pattern that drives every dihedral homomorphism construction from a (rotation, reflection) generator pair — once orderOf rotation = n is established, the four map_mul' cases of DihedralGroup n collapse to additive/subtractive arithmetic in ZMod n composed with the powered conjugation form (S3b-prep style) for the sr cases.
**Quotient-by-D_6 formulation**: framing `HexagonLabeling := Sym(6) ⧸ ⟨hexRot, hexRev⟩` makes the 60 count fall out of Lagrange directly. Avoids ad-hoc Finset enumeration of 60 orderings.

**Concrete generators via Mathlib primitives**: `hexRot = finRotate 6` and `hexRev = ⟨Fin.rev, Fin.rev, Fin.rev_rev, Fin.rev_rev⟩`. Both definitions are sorry-free, so the dihedral subgroup is fully constructive (modulo `Subgroup.closure` being noncomputable).

**Structure-encoded triples**: `SteinerPoint` and `KirkmanPoint` bundle the concurrence point with a 3-element `Finset HexagonLabeling` + a card-3 proof + concurrence-on-each-Pascal-line proof. The structures are statement-only in S1 but constrain S2+ to produce concrete witnesses.

**Concurrence routes via Cayley-Bacharach**: each Steiner / Kirkman triple corresponds to a pair of degenerate cubics that share 9 intersection points, 6 of them on the conic. The Cayley-Bacharach axiom (`conic_implies_pascal_constraint` in the parent file) extends naturally to give concurrence — but each triple requires its own algebraic setup.

**S_6 outer automorphism (Conway-Ryba 2012)**: a deeper insight is that the 20 Steiner triples form the orbits of the outer automorphism of S_6 on the 6 'syntheme totals'. This combinatorial frame would massively shorten the S2 enumeration but requires `S_6` outer-automorphism infrastructure not yet in Mathlib.

**orderOf_eq_iff is the cleanest path to exact-order proofs on small finite perm groups**: avoids manually constructing the cyclic subgroup; just exhibit the n-th power = 1 + that all smaller powers ≠ 1. The latter unrolls via `interval_cases` to native_decide per case.
mathlibGaps: No fundamental gaps — `Subgroup.closure`, `QuotientGroup`, `finRotate`, `Fin.rev`, `Subgroup.card_eq_card_quotient_mul_card_subgroup` (Lagrange) are all available.

`S_6` outer automorphism is NOT in Mathlib. The Conway-Ryba combinatorial framework for Steiner triples is therefore not available as a Mathlib shortcut; OQ-03-OQ-03 must either re-derive it or fall back to direct enumeration.
